entries.meaning: Sung by voices alone, without musical instruments. ---
examples: She joined an a cappella group in college.
The last song on the album is a cappella.
They gave an a cappella performance of the national anthem.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an a cappella group; after a verb: the whole album is a cappella
entries.form: from Italian a cappella, 'in the style of the chapel'
entries.contrast: In They sang a cappella the phrase is an adverb, the most common use; the adjective is the one before a noun or after be.

entries.meaning: Chosen and paid for item by item, not as part of a set meal or package. ---
examples: The a la carte menu is more expensive than the lunch special.
At this steakhouse the side dishes are a la carte.
More people want a la carte streaming plans instead of big bundles.
entries.type: classifying — how things are priced and sold
entries.position: both — an a la carte menu; everything here is a la carte
entries.form: from French à la carte, 'by the menu'; Americans usually write it without the accent
entries.contrast: In You can order a la carte the phrase is an adverb. Outside restaurants it means 'chosen one by one': a la carte cable channels.

entries.meaning: Served with a scoop of ice cream on top or on the side. ---
examples: I'll have the apple pie a la mode, please.
The diner is famous for its peach cobbler a la mode.
Do you want your brownie a la mode?
entries.position: after the noun — pie a la mode, never a la mode pie
entries.form: from French à la mode, 'in the fashion'
entries.contrast: A trap for anyone who knows French: in American English it almost always means 'served with ice cream', not 'fashionable'.

entries.meaning: Based on reasoning or assumptions rather than on observation or experience. ---
examples: Philosophers argue about whether math is a priori knowledge.
There's no a priori reason to think the new drug won't work.
His argument rests on a few a priori assumptions about human nature.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a priori knowledge; after a verb: the claim is a priori

entries.meaning: Completely fine; in perfect order. ---
examples: The doctor said I'm A-OK to go back to work.
Don't worry, the car is A-OK now.
She gave us the A-OK sign from the stage.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: everything is A-OK; before a noun: an A-OK job
entries.form: A + OK, first used in the US space program

entries.meaning: Abandoned has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Kids used to play in the abandoned warehouse by the river.
Police found an abandoned car on the side of the highway.
The old mining town looks completely abandoned.
The shelter takes in abandoned dogs and cats.
He felt abandoned when his father moved away.

senses.head: Left empty and no longer used or looked after
examples: Kids used to play in the abandoned warehouse by the river.
Police found an abandoned car on the side of the highway.
The old mining town looks completely abandoned.

senses.head: Left alone by the people who should take care of it
examples: The shelter takes in abandoned dogs and cats.
He felt abandoned when his father moved away.

entries.position: both — an abandoned house; the factory has been abandoned for years

entries.meaning: Embarrassed or ashamed, especially after being caught or corrected. ---
examples: He looked a little abashed when the teacher read his note out loud.
She was not the least bit abashed by the criticism.
The boys stood there, abashed, while their mother cleaned up the mess.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: she looked abashed; also an abashed smile
entries.contrast: The opposite unabashed (an unabashed fan) is more common today than abashed itself.

entries.meaning: Made shorter than the full form or the usual length. ---
examples: "Dept." is the abbreviated form of "department."
Because of the storm, the game was played in an abbreviated season.
We only had time for an abbreviated meeting.
entries.position: both — an abbreviated version; the name is often abbreviated

entries.meaning: In or relating to the stomach area of the body. ---
examples: He went to the ER with severe abdominal pain.
These exercises strengthen your abdominal muscles.
The doctor ordered an abdominal ultrasound.
entries.position: attributive only — abdominal pain; after a verb say in the abdomen
entries.contrast: The plural noun abdominals (or abs) means the stomach muscles: work on your abs.

entries.meaning: Different from what is normal or expected, usually in a bad way. ---
examples: Scientists threw out one aberrant result from the study.
His aberrant behavior worried his teachers.
One cold week in July is not that aberrant for this city.
entries.position: both — aberrant behavior; the result was aberrant

entries.meaning: Morally unacceptable and causing strong disgust. ---
examples: Racism is abhorrent to everyone in this room.
The report described abhorrent conditions at the prison.
Of all his crimes, lying to the families was the most abhorrent.
entries.position: both — an abhorrent practice; the idea is abhorrent to me
entries.takes: to + person: abhorrent to most voters

entries.meaning: Lasting for a long time and not changing. ---
examples: She has an abiding love of the ocean.
His abiding interest in history started with his grandfather's stories.
Our abiding memory of that trip is the kindness of strangers.
entries.position: attributive only — an abiding love; after a verb say lasting
entries.contrast: Law-abiding (a law-abiding citizen) comes from abide by 'obey' and has a different meaning.

entries.meaning: Abject has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Millions of people still live in abject poverty.
The launch was an abject failure.
He made an abject apology to the whole team.
She looked at him with abject fear.

senses.head: Extremely bad and without hope, used about poverty, misery or failure
examples: Millions of people still live in abject poverty.
The launch was an abject failure.

senses.head: Showing no pride or self-respect
examples: He made an abject apology to the whole team.
She looked at him with abject fear.

entries.position: attributive only — abject poverty, an abject apology

entries.meaning: Physically strong and healthy, without a disability. ---
examples: The program requires able-bodied adults to work or look for work.
We need every able-bodied volunteer to fill sandbags.
Some of the buildings were designed only for people who are able-bodied.
entries.position: both — able-bodied adults; anyone who is able-bodied can help

entries.meaning: Different from what is usual or expected, often in a way that suggests a problem. ---
examples: The blood test showed some abnormal results.
It's not abnormal for toddlers to throw tantrums.
This has been the most abnormal winter anyone can remember.
entries.position: both — abnormal results; his heart rate was abnormal
entries.contrast: Abnormal is formal and often medical. For a strange person in everyday speech Americans say weird or strange; calling someone abnormal sounds insulting.

entries.meaning: Extremely bad, unpleasant or wrong. ---
examples: The way they treated those workers was abominable.
We had abominable weather the whole week.
It was the most abominable meal I've ever paid for.
entries.position: both — abominable weather; the service was abominable

entries.meaning: Aboriginal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Canada recognizes the rights of its aboriginal peoples.
The island still has patches of aboriginal forest.
The museum has a large collection of Aboriginal art.
She studies Aboriginal languages of northern Australia.

senses.head: Living or existing in a place from the earliest times, before anyone arrived from elsewhere
examples: Canada recognizes the rights of its aboriginal peoples.
The island still has patches of aboriginal forest.

senses.head: Relating to the first peoples of Australia; written with a capital A
examples: The museum has a large collection of Aboriginal art.
She studies Aboriginal languages of northern Australia.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: aboriginal peoples
entries.contrast: For Australia it is capitalized: Aboriginal art. About Native Americans, Americans say Native American or Indigenous, not aboriginal.

entries.meaning: Failing before it could be completed. ---
examples: After an abortive attempt to fix the sink, he called a plumber.
The general was jailed after an abortive coup.
Their abortive peace talks ended after two days.
entries.position: attributive only — an abortive attempt; after a verb say failed or unsuccessful
entries.contrast: Despite the look of the word, it has nothing to do with medical abortion in everyday use; it means a plan or attempt that failed.

entries.meaning: Mentioned earlier in the same document or text. ---
examples: Please send the above-mentioned forms by Friday.
The above-mentioned tenant has not paid rent since March.
None of the above-mentioned problems have been fixed.
entries.contrast: Formal, used in letters, contracts and reports. The above-mentioned can also stand alone as a noun: the above-mentioned will attend.

entries.meaning: Honest and legal, with nothing hidden. ---
examples: I checked, and the whole sale was completely aboveboard.
He promised the investors that everything was aboveboard.
We want an aboveboard process that the public can trust.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: the deal was aboveboard; also an aboveboard deal
entries.form: compound — above + board, from card players keeping their hands above the table

entries.meaning: Built or located above the surface of the ground. ---
examples: We bought an aboveground pool for the backyard.
The city is replacing aboveground power lines with buried cables.
Most of the tank is aboveground, so it's easy to inspect.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an aboveground pool; after a verb: the pipes are aboveground

entries.meaning: Abrasive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Don't use an abrasive sponge on nonstick pans.
Sandpaper is abrasive by design.
The new manager's abrasive style upset the whole office.
He's smart, but he can be more abrasive than he realizes.

senses.head: Rough enough to scratch or rub a surface clean
examples: Don't use an abrasive sponge on nonstick pans.
Sandpaper is abrasive by design.

senses.head: Rude and harsh in a way that annoys people
examples: The new manager's abrasive style upset the whole office.
He's smart, but he can be more abrasive than he realizes.

entries.position: both — an abrasive cleaner; her manner can be abrasive

entries.meaning: Made shorter by removing parts, used about books, speeches and recordings. ---
examples: I listened to the abridged audiobook on the drive.
The school uses an abridged edition of the novel.
Be careful: the copy on the website is abridged.
entries.position: both — an abridged edition; this version is abridged

entries.meaning: Abrupt has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bus came to an abrupt stop.
Her career came to an abrupt end after the scandal.
The change in weather was more abrupt than forecasters expected.
Sorry if I was abrupt on the phone; I was in a hurry.
He gave an abrupt answer and walked away.

senses.head: Sudden and unexpected
examples: The bus came to an abrupt stop.
Her career came to an abrupt end after the scandal.
The change in weather was more abrupt than forecasters expected.

senses.head: Speaking or acting in a short way that seems rude or unfriendly
examples: Sorry if I was abrupt on the phone; I was in a hurry.
He gave an abrupt answer and walked away.

entries.position: both — an abrupt stop; his answer was abrupt

entries.meaning: Forgetful because your thoughts are somewhere else. ---
examples: My absentminded uncle left his keys in the front door again.
I'm getting more absentminded every year.
She gave me an absentminded nod and kept reading.
entries.form: compound — absent + mind + -ed; also written absent-minded

entries.meaning: Absolute has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The house was an absolute mess after the party.
That's absolute nonsense, and you know it.
We waited in absolute silence.
The king had absolute power over his people.
Freedom of speech is important, but it is not absolute.
In absolute terms, the company earned more this year.
The absolute value of -5 is 5.

senses.head: Complete and total, used to make a noun stronger
examples: The house was an absolute mess after the party.
That's absolute nonsense, and you know it.
We waited in absolute silence.

senses.head: Not limited or controlled in any way
examples: The king had absolute power over his people.
Freedom of speech is important, but it is not absolute.

senses.head: Measured on its own, not in comparison with something else
examples: In absolute terms, the company earned more this year.
The absolute value of -5 is 5.

entries.position: both — the 'complete' sense only before a noun: an absolute mess; the others also after a verb: his power was absolute
entries.contrast: The adverb absolutely is far more common in speech: Absolutely! means 'yes, definitely'.

entries.meaning: Absolutist has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The country was under absolutist rule for two centuries.
Historians compare the two absolutist monarchies.
She takes an absolutist position on privacy.
His views became more absolutist as he got older.

senses.head: Believing that a ruler or government should have unlimited power
examples: The country was under absolutist rule for two centuries.
Historians compare the two absolutist monarchies.

senses.head: Holding a principle so firmly that no exceptions are allowed
examples: She takes an absolutist position on privacy.
His views became more absolutist as he got older.

entries.position: both — an absolutist regime; her views on free speech are absolutist
entries.contrast: Also a noun: He's a free-speech absolutist.

entries.meaning: Able to soak up liquid easily. ---
examples: Use an absorbent cloth to clean up the spill.
Cotton towels are more absorbent than polyester ones.
The soil here is sandy and very absorbent.
entries.position: both — absorbent paper towels; this fabric is very absorbent
entries.contrast: Absorbent soaks up liquid; absorbing means very interesting.

entries.meaning: So interesting that it holds all your attention. ---
examples: It's an absorbing story about a family in 1930s Texas.
I found the lecture surprisingly absorbing.
Of all her novels, this is the most absorbing.
entries.position: both — an absorbing book; the documentary was absorbing
entries.form: -ing — what holds your attention; absorbed is the person who feels it
entries.contrast: The book was absorbing, but I was absorbed in the book. Absorbent is about soaking up liquid.

entries.meaning: Abstract has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Justice and freedom are abstract concepts.
Can you give me an example? This is all a bit abstract.
Algebra felt more abstract to me than geometry.
The museum's second floor is all abstract art.
Her later paintings became completely abstract.

senses.head: Based on ideas rather than on real, physical things or specific examples
examples: Justice and freedom are abstract concepts.
Can you give me an example? This is all a bit abstract.
Algebra felt more abstract to me than geometry.

senses.head: In art, using shapes and colors instead of showing people or objects as they look
examples: The museum's second floor is all abstract art.
Her later paintings became completely abstract.

entries.position: both — an abstract idea; the question is too abstract
entries.contrast: Many Americans also stress the adjective ab-STRAKT; the verb abstract is always ab-STRAKT. The noun abstract is a summary of a scientific paper.

entries.meaning: Difficult to understand because it is complicated or specialized. ---
examples: The professor lost the class in an abstruse discussion of tax law.
Most people find these legal arguments pretty abstruse.
It's one of the most abstruse books I've ever tried to read.
entries.position: both — an abstruse theory; the article was abstruse

entries.meaning: Completely unreasonable or silly. ---
examples: Twenty dollars for a hot dog? That's absurd.
It's absurd to think one person could do all this work.
The plot gets more absurd with every episode.
entries.position: both — an absurd idea; that's absurd
entries.takes: to-infinitive after it: It's absurd to charge that much; that-clause

entries.meaning: Existing in large amounts; more than enough. ---
examples: The area has abundant natural resources.
Deer are abundant in these woods.
Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe.
entries.position: both — abundant rainfall; fish are abundant in the lake
entries.takes: in + noun — having a lot of something: a region abundant in oil

entries.meaning: Treated cruelly or violently, especially over a long time. ---
examples: The center offers shelter to abused women and their kids.
They adopted an abused horse from a rescue farm.
Many of the children in the program were abused at home.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: abused children; after a verb: the dog had been abused
entries.contrast: The adjective is pronounced with /z/ (uh-BYOOZD), like the verb; the noun abuse ends in /s/.

entries.meaning: Abusive has 3 distinct senses.
examples: She finally left an abusive relationship.
He grew up with an abusive father.
The fan was thrown out for shouting abusive language at the players.
Customers who get abusive with staff will be asked to leave.
The lawsuit accuses the lender of abusive practices.
New rules target the most abusive debt collectors.

senses.head: Treating someone with cruelty or violence
examples: She finally left an abusive relationship.
He grew up with an abusive father.

senses.head: Using rude and insulting words
examples: The fan was thrown out for shouting abusive language at the players.
Customers who get abusive with staff will be asked to leave.

senses.head: Using power or a system wrongly or unfairly
examples: The lawsuit accuses the lender of abusive practices.
New rules target the most abusive debt collectors.

entries.position: both — an abusive husband; the coach was verbally abusive

entries.meaning: Full of excited talk or activity. ---
examples: The office was abuzz with news of the merger.
Social media is abuzz about the new trailer.
By noon the whole school was abuzz.
entries.position: predicative only — the town was abuzz; never before a noun

entries.meaning: Extremely bad. ---
examples: The team's defense was abysmal last night.
Customer service at that store is abysmal.
It was the most abysmal quarter in the company's history.
entries.position: both — abysmal service; the ratings were abysmal
entries.form: -al from abysm, an old form of abyss

entries.meaning: Academic has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The academic year starts in late August.
She got an academic scholarship to Stanford.
His academic record is excellent.
My brother was never very academic, but he's a great mechanic.
The program is more academic than most trade schools.
Whether we could have won is academic now.
The debate is purely academic since the store already closed.

senses.head: Relating to schools, colleges and studying
examples: The academic year starts in late August.
She got an academic scholarship to Stanford.
His academic record is excellent.

senses.head: Good at studying from books, rather than practical or technical work
examples: My brother was never very academic, but he's a great mechanic.
The program is more academic than most trade schools.

senses.head: Of theoretical interest only, because it makes no practical difference
examples: Whether we could have won is academic now.
The debate is purely academic since the store already closed.

entries.position: both — the school sense mostly before a noun: the academic year; the others also after a verb: the point is academic
entries.contrast: Russian академический отпуск is a leave of absence, not an academic vacation. The noun an academic means a university teacher or researcher.

entries.meaning: Happening or done faster than usual. ---
examples: She finished an accelerated nursing program in eighteen months.
The tree showed accelerated growth after the rain.
Smart kids are sometimes put in accelerated math classes.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an accelerated program

entries.meaning: Accented has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He speaks fluent but heavily accented English.
Her voice was soft and slightly accented.
In "banana," the middle syllable is accented.
Mark the accented syllable in each word.

senses.head: Spoken with an accent from another country or region
examples: He speaks fluent but heavily accented English.
Her voice was soft and slightly accented.

senses.head: Said with more force or stress than the syllables around it
examples: In "banana," the middle syllable is accented.
Mark the accented syllable in each word.

entries.position: both — accented English; the second syllable is accented

entries.meaning: Good enough, or allowed because most people agree it is fine. ---
examples: Is it acceptable to wear jeans to the office?
We need a solution that is acceptable to everyone.
Working from home is more acceptable now than it was ten years ago.
entries.position: both — acceptable behavior; the price is acceptable
entries.takes: to + person: acceptable to both sides; to-infinitive after it: It's not acceptable to yell at staff

entries.meaning: Generally agreed to be true, correct or normal. ---
examples: It's an accepted fact that smoking causes cancer.
Tipping twenty percent is the accepted practice in most US restaurants.
This view is now widely accepted among scientists.
entries.position: both — accepted practice; the theory is widely accepted

entries.meaning: Willing to accept people or situations as they are, without judging. ---
examples: His family was accepting when he came out.
Young people tend to be more accepting of change.
It's a small but very accepting church.
entries.position: both — an accepting community; her parents were very accepting

entries.meaning: Accessible has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The island is only accessible by boat.
All the restrooms are wheelchair accessible.
The new website is more accessible to people who are blind.
The book explains quantum physics in an accessible way.
Her music is more accessible than her early albums.

senses.head: Easy to reach, enter or use, including for people with disabilities
examples: The island is only accessible by boat.
All the restrooms are wheelchair accessible.
The new website is more accessible to people who are blind.

senses.head: Easy to understand or enjoy
examples: The book explains quantum physics in an accessible way.
Her music is more accessible than her early albums.

entries.position: both — an accessible entrance; the park is accessible by bus
entries.takes: to + person: accessible to everyone; by + means: accessible by car
entries.contrast: Russian доступный also means cheap; for price, English says affordable, not accessible.

entries.meaning: Often having accidents, falling or breaking things. ---
examples: My son is so accident-prone that the ER nurses know his name.
She's the most accident-prone person I know.
Tired drivers are more accident-prone.
entries.position: both — an accident-prone kid; I'm so accident-prone

entries.meaning: Happening by chance or by mistake, not planned. ---
examples: Penicillin was an accidental discovery.
Investigators say the fire was accidental.
The report blamed the deaths on accidental overdoses.
entries.position: both — an accidental discovery; the fire was accidental

entries.meaning: Willing to help and to change plans to fit what other people need. ---
examples: The restaurant was very accommodating about my food allergies.
My boss is accommodating when I need to leave early for my kids.
The second landlord was much more accommodating than the first.
entries.position: both — an accommodating host; the hotel staff were very accommodating

entries.meaning: Going or coming together with something else. ---
examples: Please read the accompanying instructions before you start.
The article and the accompanying photos got a lot of attention.
A fever and accompanying headache are common side effects.
entries.position: attributive only — the accompanying letter; after a verb use the verb: the letter that accompanies it

entries.meaning: Very skilled at something, usually after years of practice. ---
examples: He's an accomplished chef and a published author.
Both of her daughters are accomplished musicians.
She was the most accomplished player on the team.
entries.position: both — an accomplished pianist; she is very accomplished

entries.meaning: Expected to explain your decisions and actions and to accept blame if something goes wrong. ---
examples: The officers involved should be held accountable.
Managers are accountable for their team's results.
Voters want a more accountable city council.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: they must be held accountable; also an accountable government
entries.takes: for + what you did or are in charge of: accountable for the mistake; to + the person or group you answer to: accountable to voters
entries.contrast: The fixed phrase is hold someone accountable. Responsible is the everyday word; accountable stresses having to explain your actions and accept the consequences.

entries.meaning: Officially approved as meeting the required standards. ---
examples: Make sure the college is accredited before you pay tuition.
Only accredited journalists were allowed into the briefing.
The hospital is accredited by a national commission.
entries.position: both — an accredited university; the program is fully accredited
entries.takes: by + the official body: accredited by the state

entries.meaning: Built up gradually over time, used about money, interest and time off. ---
examples: The loan balance includes accrued interest.
You'll be paid for any accrued vacation days when you leave.
The company reported its accrued expenses for the year.
entries.position: attributive only — accrued interest; after a verb use the verb: interest has accrued

entries.meaning: Gathered or built up gradually over a period of time. ---
examples: It took a whole day to clear the accumulated snow.
The book draws on thirty years of accumulated experience.
They lost most of their accumulated savings in the crash.
entries.position: attributive only — accumulated wealth; after a verb use the verb: the snow had accumulated

entries.meaning: Suggesting that someone has done something wrong. ---
examples: Try not to use an accusatory tone when you bring it up.
Her emails got more accusatory as the project fell behind.
The letter was polite but clearly accusatory.
entries.position: both — an accusatory tone; his questions sounded accusatory

entries.meaning: Showing that you think someone has done something wrong. ---
examples: She gave me an accusing look when the cake went missing.
Everyone pointed an accusing finger at the referee.
His voice wasn't angry, just quietly accusing.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an accusing look

entries.meaning: Extremely skilled at something. ---
examples: Her dad was an ace pilot in the Air Force.
The paper hired an ace reporter from Chicago.
We need an ace mechanic to figure out that noise.
entries.position: attributive only — an ace pilot; after a verb say excellent
entries.contrast: Mostly a noun (an ace, the playing card or an expert) and a verb (I aced the test). That's ace! as praise is British; in the US the adjective goes before a noun that names a skill: an ace mechanic.

entries.meaning: Sharp and critical in a clever but unkind way, used about people, words and humor. ---
examples: The show is famous for its acerbic humor.
He wrote an acerbic review of the new restaurant.
Her comments got more acerbic as the night went on.
entries.position: both — an acerbic critic; her reviews can be acerbic

entries.meaning: Possible to do or reach with effort. ---
examples: Set small, achievable goals for each week.
Is a four-hour marathon achievable for a beginner?
Breaking the project into steps made it feel more achievable.
entries.position: both — an achievable goal; the target is achievable

entries.meaning: Aching has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A hot bath helps my aching back.
After the hike we collapsed on the couch with aching feet.
The song is full of aching sadness.
She felt an aching loneliness after he left.

senses.head: Hurting with a dull, steady pain
examples: A hot bath helps my aching back.
After the hike we collapsed on the couch with aching feet.

senses.head: Felt very strongly, as sadness or longing
examples: The song is full of aching sadness.
She felt an aching loneliness after he left.

entries.position: attributive only — aching muscles; in my back is aching the word is the verb

entries.meaning: Having dull pains in the body, often when you are sick or tired. ---
examples: I woke up tired and achy, so I think I'm getting the flu.
Cold weather makes my knees achy.
The day after the game I felt even achier.
entries.position: both — achy joints; I feel achy all over

entries.meaning: Acid has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The wine was too acid for my taste.
Lemons have an acid flavor that cuts through rich food.
The critic is known for her acid wit.
He made a few acid remarks about his former boss.
Blueberries grow best in acid soil.
The water in the lake has become more acid over the years.

senses.head: Sharp and sour in taste
examples: The wine was too acid for my taste.
Lemons have an acid flavor that cuts through rich food.

senses.head: Critical and unkind in a clever, biting way
examples: The critic is known for her acid wit.
He made a few acid remarks about his former boss.

senses.head: Containing acid; having a pH below 7
examples: Blueberries grow best in acid soil.
The water in the lake has become more acid over the years.

entries.position: both — an acid taste; the soil is acid
entries.contrast: In acid rain and acid reflux the word is a noun used before another noun. For the chemistry sense Americans more often say acidic.

entries.meaning: Acidic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Coffee and soda are both fairly acidic.
Oceans are becoming more acidic as they absorb carbon dioxide.
This orange juice is too acidic for my stomach.
Add a little sugar if the sauce tastes acidic.

senses.head: Containing acid; having a pH below 7
examples: Coffee and soda are both fairly acidic.
Oceans are becoming more acidic as they absorb carbon dioxide.

senses.head: Tasting sour and sharp
examples: This orange juice is too acidic for my stomach.
Add a little sugar if the sauce tastes acidic.

entries.position: both — acidic soil; tomatoes are acidic

entries.meaning: Generally accepted or recognized as being something. ---
examples: She is an acknowledged expert on climate policy.
He was the acknowledged leader of the group.
The risks of the plan are widely acknowledged.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: the acknowledged leader; after a verb: his talent is widely acknowledged

entries.meaning: Acoustic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He brought his acoustic guitar to the campfire.
The band played an acoustic set at the record store.
Tonight's concert is fully acoustic.
The hall's acoustic design is the best in the city.
Engineers measured the acoustic properties of the new material.

senses.head: Played without electric amplification
examples: He brought his acoustic guitar to the campfire.
The band played an acoustic set at the record store.
Tonight's concert is fully acoustic.

senses.head: Relating to sound or to how well sound carries in a place
examples: The hall's acoustic design is the best in the city.
Engineers measured the acoustic properties of the new material.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an acoustic guitar; after a verb: the show was acoustic

entries.meaning: Acquainted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Are you two acquainted?
We got acquainted at a friend's barbecue.
New employees should get acquainted with the safety rules.
After a week I was more acquainted with the neighborhood.

senses.head: Knowing someone because you have met them, though not closely
examples: Are you two acquainted?
We got acquainted at a friend's barbecue.

senses.head: Knowing about something because you have seen, read or used it
examples: New employees should get acquainted with the safety rules.
After a week I was more acquainted with the neighborhood.

entries.position: predicative only — we're acquainted, get acquainted; never before a noun
entries.takes: with + person or thing: acquainted with the neighbors, acquainted with the rules
entries.contrast: Russian знакомый before a noun is not acquainted: a familiar face, an acquaintance. The common phrase is get acquainted or get to know each other.

entries.meaning: Gained or developed during your life, not present from birth. ---
examples: Coffee is an acquired taste for most kids.
The condition is acquired, not inherited.
Reading music is an acquired skill.
entries.position: attributive only — an acquired taste; after a verb use the verb: the habit was acquired
entries.contrast: An acquired taste is something most people dislike at first but can learn to like: Blue cheese is an acquired taste.

entries.meaning: Eager to get more money, possessions or, for a company, other businesses. ---
examples: Critics say we live in an acquisitive culture.
The tech giant has been especially acquisitive this year.
He grew more acquisitive as his fortune grew.
entries.position: both — an acquisitive society; the company has become acquisitive

entries.meaning: Sharp and unpleasant to smell or taste, often burning the nose or throat. ---
examples: Acrid smoke filled the kitchen.
The air near the plant was acrid and hard to breathe.
The smell got more acrid as we got closer to the fire.
entries.position: both — acrid smoke; the air was acrid

entries.meaning: Full of anger and bitter arguments. ---
examples: They went through an acrimonious divorce.
The town hall meeting quickly turned acrimonious.
It was one of the most acrimonious campaigns in years.
entries.position: both — an acrimonious divorce; the debate became acrimonious

entries.meaning: Involving or showing difficult, athletic movements like jumping, flipping and balancing. ---
examples: The receiver made an acrobatic catch in the end zone.
The circus show was full of acrobatic stunts.
Her routine this year is even more acrobatic.
entries.position: both — an acrobatic catch; the dancers were incredibly acrobatic

entries.meaning: Affecting everyone or everything in a group equally. ---
examples: The city announced across-the-board budget cuts.
Workers got an across-the-board raise of three percent.
The new rules call for across-the-board testing in every school.
entries.position: attributive only — hyphenated before a noun: across-the-board cuts; after a verb across the board is an adverb phrase, without hyphens
entries.form: compound — preposition phrase across the board, hyphenated before a noun
entries.contrast: Prices rose across the board uses the adverb phrase; only an across-the-board increase is the adjective.

entries.meaning: Doing someone else's job for a short time, until a permanent person is chosen. ---
examples: She was named acting principal after Mr. Lee retired.
The acting police chief spoke to reporters.
He served as acting CEO for six months.
entries.form: -ing from act (to do a job for someone)
entries.contrast: Russian действующий before a job title is usually current, not acting: the current president. Acting means temporary, until someone is officially appointed. The noun acting is the profession.

entries.meaning: Actionable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The report gives managers actionable recommendations.
We need feedback that is more actionable than 'do better'.
His lawyer said the false claims were actionable.
Not every rude comment is legally actionable.

senses.head: Clear and practical enough to act on right away
examples: The report gives managers actionable recommendations.
We need feedback that is more actionable than 'do better'.

senses.head: In law, giving someone a reason to sue
examples: His lawyer said the false claims were actionable.
Not every rude comment is legally actionable.

entries.русский: практически применимый; дающий основание для иска
entries.position: both — actionable advice; the statement may be actionable

entries.meaning: Activated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Once your account is activated, you can log in.
Make sure the alarm is activated before you leave.
The phone stays locked until it is activated.
The water filter contains activated carbon.
Doctors sometimes give activated charcoal after a poisoning.

senses.head: Made ready to work, or switched on
examples: Once your account is activated, you can log in.
Make sure the alarm is activated before you leave.
The phone stays locked until it is activated.

senses.head: Treated with heat or chemicals so that it works better, as charcoal
examples: The water filter contains activated carbon.
Doctors sometimes give activated charcoal after a poisoning.

entries.position: both — activated charcoal; your new card is activated

entries.meaning: Active has 4 distinct senses.
examples: My grandmother is still very active at eighty.
Kids need to stay active during the summer.
I've been more active since I got a dog.
He's an active member of the PTA.
She has always been active in her church.
Mount St. Helens is still an active volcano.
Your account is no longer active.
Police are treating it as an active investigation.
"The dog bit the man" is in the active voice.
Editors usually prefer active verbs.

senses.head: Moving around and doing physical things; full of energy
examples: My grandmother is still very active at eighty.
Kids need to stay active during the summer.
I've been more active since I got a dog.

senses.head: Taking part in something and working hard at it
examples: He's an active member of the PTA.
She has always been active in her church.

senses.head: Working, operating or happening now
examples: Mount St. Helens is still an active volcano.
Your account is no longer active.
Police are treating it as an active investigation.

senses.head: In grammar, having a subject that does the action of the verb
examples: "The dog bit the man" is in the active voice.
Editors usually prefer active verbs.

entries.position: both — an active lifestyle; she's very active
entries.takes: in + noun or -ing — taking part: active in local politics
entries.opposite: inactive; for the body, sedentary; in grammar, passive
entries.contrast: Russian активный is often active, but активный отдых is an active vacation or outdoor activities, and активные продажи is proactive sales.

entries.meaning: Working hard and openly to bring about political, social or business change. ---
examples: Critics call her an activist judge.
An activist investor bought a large stake in the company.
The Supreme Court became more activist in the 1960s.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an activist judge; after a verb: the court has become more activist
entries.contrast: Usually a noun (a climate activist). The adjective is common in US politics and business: an activist judge makes new policy through rulings; activist investors push a company to change.

entries.meaning: Relating to calculating risks and costs for insurance and pensions. ---
examples: Insurers use actuarial tables to set life insurance prices.
She passed her first actuarial exam in college.
The pension fund hired an actuarial firm to review its numbers.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with Russian актуальный (current, relevant). That is relevant, topical or up-to-date.

entries.meaning: Acute has 4 distinct senses.

The housing crisis is most acute in big cities.
She felt acute embarrassment when her phone rang during the funeral.
He was rushed to the hospital with acute appendicitis.
The clinic treats acute injuries, not long-term conditions.

She's an acute observer of small-town life.
Draw an acute angle and label it.
Every triangle has at least two acute angles.

senses.head: Very serious or severe
examples: There is an acute shortage of nurses in rural hospitals.
The housing crisis is most acute in big cities.
She felt acute embarrassment when her phone rang during the funeral.

senses.head: In medicine, starting suddenly and quickly becoming severe
examples: He was rushed to the hospital with acute appendicitis.
The clinic treats acute injuries, not long-term conditions.

senses.head: Very sensitive or sharp, used about the senses and the mind
examples: Dogs have an acute sense of smell.
She's an acute observer of small-town life.

senses.head: In geometry, less than 90 degrees
examples: Draw an acute angle and label it.
Every triangle has at least two acute angles.

entries.position: both — an acute shortage; the problem is acute

entries.meaning: Made or done for one particular purpose or situation, often without planning. ---
examples: The board formed an ad hoc committee to study the problem.
Our hiring process is too ad hoc; we need clear rules.
The repairs were done on an ad hoc basis.
entries.русский: специальный, созданный для конкретной цели; импровизированный
entries.position: both — an ad hoc committee; the process was pretty ad hoc
entries.comparison: more/most — more ad hoc, most ad hoc
entries.contrast: In decisions were made ad hoc it is an adverb. The adjective can sound negative: 'unplanned, not systematic'.

entries.meaning: Attacking the person who makes an argument instead of the argument itself. ---
examples: Calling her stupid is an ad hominem attack, not a counterargument.
The debate turned into a series of ad hominem insults.
Please avoid ad hominem comments in this forum.
entries.position: attributive only — an ad hominem attack

entries.meaning: Refusing to change your opinion or decision. ---
examples: He was adamant that he had locked the door.
My parents were adamant about finishing college first.
She became even more adamant after reading the report.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: she was adamant; also an adamant refusal
entries.takes: about + noun or -ing: adamant about staying; that-clause: adamant that he was innocent
entries.contrast: Stress the first syllable: AD-uh-muhnt. It describes a person's position, not a hard material, in modern English.

entries.meaning: Able to change or be changed easily to fit new situations. ---
examples: Raccoons are adaptable animals that do well in cities.
We need someone adaptable who can handle last-minute changes.
Younger workers are often more adaptable to new technology.
entries.position: both — an adaptable employee; kids are very adaptable

entries.meaning: Adaptive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The new car has adaptive cruise control.
The software uses adaptive learning to match each student's level.
The resort offers adaptive skiing lessons.
Her school provides adaptive equipment for students who need it.

senses.head: Designed to change and adjust to different conditions or needs
examples: The new car has adaptive cruise control.
The software uses adaptive learning to match each student's level.

senses.head: Made for people with disabilities so they can take part in an activity
examples: The resort offers adaptive skiing lessons.
Her school provides adaptive equipment for students who need it.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: adaptive equipment; after a verb: the system is adaptive
entries.contrast: Adaptable describes a person or thing that can change; adaptive is more technical — designed to adjust, or helping someone adjust: adaptive cruise control, adaptive sports.

entries.meaning: Causing a strong need to keep using or doing it. ---
examples: Nicotine is highly addictive.
These chips are dangerously addictive.
Some experts say social media is more addictive than TV.
entries.position: both — an addictive drug; this game is addictive
entries.contrast: Addictive is the thing that causes the habit; addicted is the person who has it: The app is addictive, and I'm addicted to it.

entries.meaning: Added to what already exists; extra. ---
examples: There's an additional fee for checked bags.
For additional information, visit our website.
Delivery is available, but the cost is additional.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: additional costs; after a verb: shipping is additional

entries.meaning: Confused and unable to think clearly. ---
examples: After two nights without sleep, my brain was completely addled.
He gave a rambling, addled speech.
The medicine left her more addled than before.
entries.position: both — an addled mind; my brain is totally addled
entries.form: -ed from addle; common in compounds: drug-addled, sleep-addled

entries.meaning: Very good at doing something that takes skill. ---
examples: He's adept at getting kids to eat vegetables.
She is an adept politician.
Teenagers are often more adept with technology than their parents.
entries.position: both — an adept negotiator; she's adept at handling clients
entries.takes: at + noun or -ing: adept at fixing things; in + noun: adept in several languages
entries.contrast: The adjective is stressed uh-DEPT. The noun adept (an expert) is often AD-ept, and Russian адепт (a follower) is closer to follower or devotee.

entries.meaning: Adequate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Make sure you get adequate sleep before the exam.
The apartment is small but adequate for two people.
Many schools still lack adequate funding.
The food was adequate, but nothing special.
His performance was adequate at best.

senses.head: Enough in amount or good enough for a particular need
examples: Make sure you get adequate sleep before the exam.
The apartment is small but adequate for two people.
Many schools still lack adequate funding.

senses.head: Acceptable but not especially good
examples: The food was adequate, but nothing special.
His performance was adequate at best.

entries.position: both — adequate funding; the space is adequate
entries.takes: for + noun: adequate for our needs; to-infinitive: adequate to cover the costs
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian адекватный about a person (sane, reasonable) is reasonable, sensible or normal. English adequate means 'enough' or 'just OK'. Stress: AD-i-kwuht, not ad-e-KWAYT.

entries.meaning: Able to stick to a surface; sticky. ---
examples: Put an adhesive bandage on the cut.
The hooks have an adhesive back, so you don't need nails.
Peel off the paper to expose the adhesive side.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: adhesive tape; after a verb: the back of the label is adhesive
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a strong adhesive (a glue).

entries.meaning: Next to or very near something else. ---
examples: The hotel is adjacent to the convention center.
We booked adjacent rooms so the kids could be near us.
Firefighters kept the fire from spreading to adjacent buildings.
entries.position: both — an adjacent room; the parking lot is adjacent to the school
entries.takes: to + noun: adjacent to the park

entries.meaning: Adjunct has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He works as an adjunct professor at two community colleges.
Many adjunct instructors don't get health insurance.
The drug is used as an adjunct therapy alongside surgery.
The online course is an adjunct program to the main degree.

senses.head: Working at a college on a part-time or temporary contract, not as permanent staff
examples: He works as an adjunct professor at two community colleges.
Many adjunct instructors don't get health insurance.

senses.head: Added to something more important, as a support
examples: The drug is used as an adjunct therapy alongside surgery.
The online course is an adjunct program to the main degree.

entries.contrast: In US universities an adjunct professor is a part-time, non-permanent teacher, not a senior rank. Russian адъюнкт is a different, military-academic title.

entries.meaning: Possible to change in size, height or position. ---
examples: I bought an adjustable desk so I can stand while I work.
The seat height is fully adjustable.
The straps on this backpack are adjustable.
entries.position: both — an adjustable chair; the straps are adjustable

entries.meaning: Adjusted has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Adjusted for inflation, wages have barely grown.
The adjusted numbers show a smaller loss.
After a month, the kids were fully adjusted to the new school.
She's one of the best-adjusted people I know.

senses.head: Changed slightly to allow for a particular factor, used about numbers
examples: Adjusted for inflation, wages have barely grown.
The adjusted numbers show a smaller loss.

senses.head: Used to a new situation and comfortable in it; emotionally stable
examples: After a month, the kids were fully adjusted to the new school.
She's one of the best-adjusted people I know.

entries.position: both — adjusted figures; prices adjusted for inflation; he seems well adjusted
entries.comparison: not gradable — but well-adjusted grades: better-adjusted, best-adjusted
entries.takes: for + noun — corrected to allow for something: adjusted for inflation; to + noun — used to something new: adjusted to the time change

entries.meaning: Relating to managing and organizing the work of a business or organization. ---
examples: She works as an administrative assistant at a law firm.
Too much of a teacher's time goes to administrative tasks.
The officer was placed on administrative leave.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: administrative staff; after a verb: the delay was purely administrative
entries.contrast: Administrative leave in the US is time off, often paid, while an employee is investigated. Russian административный штраф is usually just a fine.

entries.meaning: Deserving respect and approval. ---
examples: She did an admirable job under difficult conditions.
His loyalty to his friends is admirable.
What makes her story more admirable is that she never complained.
entries.position: both — an admirable goal; his honesty is admirable
entries.contrast: The stress moves: adMIRE, but ADmirable.

entries.meaning: Allowed to be used or considered, especially as evidence in a court of law. ---
examples: The judge ruled that the confession was not admissible.
Lie detector results are rarely admissible in court.
The lawyers argued over which documents were admissible evidence.
entries.position: both — admissible evidence; the recording is not admissible

entries.meaning: Adolescent has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The clinic specializes in adolescent mental health.
Adolescent girls are especially at risk.
The senator's adolescent jokes embarrassed his staff.
Their feud is getting more adolescent every week.

senses.head: Relating to young people between childhood and adulthood
examples: The clinic specializes in adolescent mental health.
Adolescent girls are especially at risk.

senses.head: Behaving in a silly or immature way for an adult
examples: The senator's adolescent jokes embarrassed his staff.
Their feud is getting more adolescent every week.

entries.position: both — adolescent boys; his humor is a little adolescent
entries.contrast: Also a noun: an adolescent. In everyday speech Americans say teenage or teen for the first sense.

entries.meaning: Ready and available to be adopted, especially a pet from a shelter. ---

Older children are just as adoptable as babies.

entries.position: both — adoptable pets; all these puppies are adoptable

She speaks proudly of her adopted country.

examples: They have two biological kids and one adopted daughter.
She didn't find out she was adopted until she was twenty.

senses.head: Chosen as your own, though not where you were born
examples: Chicago is his adopted hometown.
She speaks proudly of her adopted country.

entries.position: both — an adopted daughter; I was adopted

entries.meaning: Having legally taken a child into the family as their own. ---
examples: His adoptive parents were at the wedding.
She has a close relationship with her adoptive family.
Adoptive mothers can get paid leave at many companies.
entries.contrast: Adoptive is the family who adopts; adopted is the child. ✗ his adopted parents → his adoptive parents.

entries.meaning: Very cute and easy to love, especially a child or small animal. ---
examples: Look at that adorable puppy!
Your little boy is absolutely adorable.
That was the most adorable wedding I've ever been to.

entries.meaning: Showing great love or admiration for someone. ---
examples: The singer waved to thousands of adoring fans.
She gave her husband an adoring look.
The grandparents couldn't have been more adoring.

entries.meaning: Skillful and quick, especially in handling people or difficult situations. ---
examples: She's an adroit negotiator.
He was adroit at avoiding hard questions.
No one in the White House was more adroit with the press.

entries.meaning: Adult has 3 distinct senses.
examples: They have two adult children who live out of state.
An adult ticket costs twenty dollars.
Most of his adult life was spent in Chicago.

The site has a warning about adult content.
That was a very adult way to handle the argument.
Let's try to be adult about this.

senses.head: Fully grown or of legal age
examples: They have two adult children who live out of state.
An adult ticket costs twenty dollars.
Most of his adult life was spent in Chicago.

senses.head: Intended for adults only, usually because it shows sex
examples: The hotel blocks adult channels.
The site has a warning about adult content.

senses.head: Mature and sensible, as a grown-up should be

entries.meaning: Made weaker or less pure by adding something of lower quality. ---
examples: The honey turned out to be adulterated with corn syrup.
Police seized a shipment of adulterated drugs.
The FDA can recall food it finds adulterated.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with adult or adultery in meaning. The opposite unadulterated is more common, often figuratively: pure, unadulterated joy.

entries.meaning: Involving sex between a married person and someone who is not their husband or wife. ---
examples: The senator's adulterous affair ended his career.
She left her adulterous husband.
The relationship was adulterous from the start.

entries.meaning: Advance has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We need at least two weeks' advance notice.

The president's advance team arrived a week early.
An advance party checked the campsite.

examples: We need at least two weeks' advance notice.
Advance tickets are cheaper than tickets at the door.
The storm came with very little advance warning.

senses.head: Going ahead of the main group to prepare
examples: The president's advance team arrived a week early.
An advance party checked the campsite.

entries.contrast: Advance means beforehand: advance notice, advance tickets. Advanced means at a high level or far along: an advanced course. ✗ advanced booking → advance booking. In advance is an adverb phrase, and advance is also a noun and a verb.

senses.head: Modern and highly developed
examples: The hospital uses the most advanced equipment in the state.

This class is for advanced students only.
His English is quite advanced.

senses.head: Far along in development or time
examples: The cancer was already at an advanced stage.

entries.meaning: Giving an advantage; helpful or favorable. ---

Buying in the spring is more advantageous than waiting until summer.
entries.contrast: The stress moves: AD-van-tij, but ad-vuhn-TAY-juhs.

entries.meaning: Willing to take risks and try new things. ---
examples: Adventuresome travelers can hike to the top.
The menu is for adventuresome eaters.
She's more adventuresome than her brother.
entries.contrast: Mostly American. It means the same as adventurous, which is far more common.

entries.meaning: Adventurous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'm not very adventurous when it comes to food.

The architect has a bold, adventurous style.
They planned an adventurous trip through the Andes.
His early life was pretty adventurous.

senses.head: Willing to try new or risky things
examples: I'm not very adventurous when it comes to food.
Kids get more adventurous as they get older.
The architect has a bold, adventurous style.

senses.head: Full of excitement, new experiences and some danger
examples: They planned an adventurous trip through the Andes.
His early life was pretty adventurous.

entries.meaning: Harmful or unfavorable. ---
examples: The drug has few adverse side effects.
Flights were canceled because of adverse weather.

entries.meaning: Giving advice but without the power to make decisions. ---
examples: She sits on the company's advisory board.
The committee's role is purely advisory.
He was hired in an advisory capacity.
entries.contrast: An advisory is also an American noun for an official warning: a winter storm advisory, a travel advisory.

entries.meaning: Aerial has 2 distinct senses.

The drone gives you an aerial view of the whole farm.
Aerial surveys found the missing hikers.
The circus ended with an aerial act.

senses.head: Seen or taken from an aircraft or from high above
examples: The aerial photos show how much of the town flooded.
The drone gives you an aerial view of the whole farm.
Aerial surveys found the missing hikers.

senses.head: Happening in the air
examples: The circus ended with an aerial act.
The army began an aerial attack at dawn.

entries.contrast: In British English an aerial is a TV or radio antenna; Americans say antenna.

entries.meaning: Aerobic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Swimming is great aerobic exercise.

Aerobic bacteria break down the waste.
The process is aerobic, so the tank needs air.

senses.head: Of exercise that makes the heart and lungs work harder for a long time
examples: Swimming is great aerobic exercise.
Try to get thirty minutes of aerobic activity a day.
Walking fast is aerobic if you keep it up.

senses.head: Of living things or processes that need oxygen
examples: Aerobic bacteria break down the waste.
The process is aerobic, so the tank needs air.

entries.meaning: Aerodynamic has 2 distinct senses.

Engineers ran aerodynamic tests on the wing.
Aerodynamic drag slows the car down at high speed.

senses.head: Shaped so that it moves easily through the air
examples: The new model is more aerodynamic, so it uses less gas.
Cyclists wear aerodynamic helmets in races.
The car's shape is very aerodynamic.

senses.head: Relating to how air moves around objects
examples: Engineers ran aerodynamic tests on the wing.
Aerodynamic drag slows the car down at high speed.

entries.meaning: Relating to the science of building and flying aircraft. ---
examples: He has a degree in aeronautical engineering.
The museum has a large aeronautical collection.
Pilots have to read aeronautical charts.

entries.meaning: Turned into very fine drops or particles that float in the air. ---
examples: The virus can spread through aerosolized droplets.
Some medicines are given in aerosolized form.
Once the chemical is aerosolized, it's hard to contain.

entries.meaning: Aesthetic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The building has little aesthetic value.

It was a practical choice, not an aesthetic one.
The café is very aesthetic, so it's popular on Instagram.
She rearranged the shelves to make them look more aesthetic.

senses.head: Relating to beauty, art and how things look
examples: The building has little aesthetic value.
We chose the tiles for aesthetic reasons.
It was a practical choice, not an aesthetic one.

senses.head: Pleasing to look at
examples: The café is very aesthetic, so it's popular on Instagram.
She rearranged the shelves to make them look more aesthetic.

entries.comparison: not gradable — sense 2 informally more aesthetic
entries.contrast: Also spelled esthetic in American English, especially in medicine and beauty (esthetician). Aesthetic is also a noun for a style: the minimalist aesthetic.

entries.meaning: Friendly, relaxed and easy to talk to. ---
examples: Our new neighbor is an affable retired teacher.
He seemed affable enough on the phone.
She's the most affable person in the office.

entries.meaning: Affected has 2 distinct senses.

Everyone affected by the layoffs will get severance.
She spoke with an affected British accent.
His politeness seemed a little affected.

senses.head: Influenced or harmed by something
examples: Aid is being sent to the affected areas.
The most affected families lost their homes.
Everyone affected by the layoffs will get severance.

senses.head: Not natural; done to impress people
examples: She spoke with an affected British accent.
His politeness seemed a little affected.

entries.position: both — sense 1 also after the noun: the areas affected
entries.comparison: not gradable — except sense 2: more affected, most affected

entries.meaning: Showing love and warm feelings. ---
examples: Our cat is very affectionate with kids.

My second dog is more affectionate than the first.

entries.meaning: Officially connected to a larger group or organization. ---
examples: The clinic is affiliated with the university hospital.
Local affiliated stations will carry the game.
He isn't affiliated with any political party.

entries.meaning: Affirmative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We need an affirmative answer by Friday.
The vote was affirmative.
He gave an affirmative nod.
Change the affirmative sentences into questions.
In affirmative sentences we use some, not any.

senses.head: Meaning or saying yes
examples: We need an affirmative answer by Friday.
The vote was affirmative.
