entries.position: attributive only — after the noun in God Almighty
entries.form: all + mighty, written with one l
entries.contrast: The almighty dollar is an American phrase criticizing the power of money. God Almighty! is also an exclamation of surprise or anger, which some people find offensive.

entries.meaning: Unfriendly and not wanting to get involved with other people. ---
examples: The new manager seemed cold and aloof.
She kept herself aloof from office gossip.
Cats are often more aloof than dogs.

entries.meaning: Dominant and confident, acting as the leader of a group. ---
examples: He thinks he's the alpha male of the office.
The alpha wolf eats first.
She comes across as very alpha in meetings.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: an alpha male
entries.contrast: Mostly heard in alpha male and alpha female. As a noun, alpha is the Greek letter and an early test version of software; in an alpha release that noun is only a modifier.

entries.meaning: Arranged in the order of the letters of the alphabet. ---
examples: Put the names in alphabetical order.
The guest list is alphabetical by last name.
There's an alphabetical index at the back of the book.

entries.meaning: Put in alphabetical order. ---
examples: She keeps an alphabetized list of every book she's read.
Are the files alphabetized by name or by date?
His spice rack is perfectly alphabetized.

entries.meaning: Made up of both letters and numbers. ---
examples: Your password must be at least eight alphanumeric characters.
Each package gets an alphanumeric tracking code.
The serial number is alphanumeric, so watch for the letter O versus zero.

entries.meaning: Found in or typical of high mountains. ---
examples: We hiked through alpine meadows full of wildflowers.
The lake sits in an alpine valley in the Rockies.
Few trees grow in the alpine zone above eleven thousand feet.
entries.contrast: Lowercase alpine describes any high mountains (alpine lakes in Colorado); capital Alpine means the Alps in Europe. Alpine skiing is downhill skiing.

entries.meaning: Changed, so that it is different from what it was. ---
examples: The bank spotted an altered signature on the check.
Some drugs produce an altered state of consciousness.
Her whole manner seemed altered after the trip.

entries.meaning: Happening or arranged by turns, first one thing and then the other. ---
examples: The floor has alternating black and white tiles.
Outlets in the US supply alternating current.
The forecast calls for alternating rain and sun.
entries.contrast: The adjective alternate is a different word: on alternate days means every other day, and an alternate route is a substitute one.

entries.meaning: Caring about other people's good more than your own. ---
examples: Her reasons for volunteering were purely altruistic.
It was an altruistic gesture, and he expected nothing back.
Some animals show surprisingly altruistic behavior.

entries.meaning: Amateur has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He's an amateur photographer with a real eye.
The amateur league plays on Saturday mornings.
The website looks really amateur.
Their second video looked even more amateur than the first.

senses.head: Doing something for pleasure, not as a paid job
examples: He's an amateur photographer with a real eye.
The amateur league plays on Saturday mornings.

senses.head: Done without skill; not looking professional
examples: The website looks really amateur.
Their second video looked even more amateur than the first.

entries.comparison: more/most — more amateur, only in sense 2
entries.contrast: Also a noun: She's an amateur. For the negative meaning, amateurish is more common in writing.

entries.meaning: Done badly, without the skill of a professional. ---
examples: The acting was painfully amateurish.
It was an amateurish mistake for someone with his experience.
The most amateurish part of the film was the sound.

entries.meaning: Having the deep yellow-orange color of amber. ---
examples: The beer poured a clear amber color.
Her eyes looked almost amber in the sunlight.
Amber streetlights lined the old road.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the fossil resin itself. Americans call the middle traffic light yellow; amber there is British.

entries.meaning: Able to use both hands equally well; of a tool, made for either hand. ---
examples: The pitcher is ambidextrous and can throw with either arm.
Only about one percent of people are truly ambidextrous.
The mouse has an ambidextrous design, so lefties can use it too.

entries.meaning: Ambient has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Store the medicine at ambient temperature.
The camera works well even in low ambient light.
Ambient noise from the highway makes it hard to sleep.
The spa plays soft ambient music all day.
He records ambient tracks for video games.

senses.head: Present in the surrounding area
examples: Store the medicine at ambient temperature.
The camera works well even in low ambient light.
Ambient noise from the highway makes it hard to sleep.

senses.head: Of music or sound: quiet and atmospheric, meant for the background
examples: The spa plays soft ambient music all day.
He records ambient tracks for video games.

entries.meaning: Having more than one possible meaning; not clear. ---
examples: The wording of the contract is ambiguous.
She gave an ambiguous answer, and I still don't know if she's coming.
The ending of the movie is deliberately ambiguous.

entries.meaning: Having mixed feelings about something, both positive and negative. ---
examples: I'm still ambivalent about moving to Denver.
Many voters feel ambivalent toward both candidates.
She has an ambivalent relationship with her hometown.
entries.contrast: Not indifferent: an ambivalent person has feelings both ways, not no feelings. ambiguous describes meaning, not feelings.

entries.meaning: Ambulatory has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The patient is ambulatory and can go home tomorrow.
Ambulatory residents eat in the main dining room.
The clinic offers ambulatory surgery.
Ambulatory care centers are opening all over the suburbs.

senses.head: Of a patient: able to walk
examples: The patient is ambulatory and can go home tomorrow.
Ambulatory residents eat in the main dining room.

senses.head: Of medical care: given to patients who do not stay overnight in the hospital
examples: The clinic offers ambulatory surgery.
Ambulatory care centers are opening all over the suburbs.

entries.position: both — sense 2 only before a noun

entries.meaning: Amenable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My boss is amenable to working from home on Fridays.
They seemed amenable to a lower price.
The condition is amenable to surgery.
Not every problem is amenable to a quick fix.

senses.head: Willing to accept or agree to something
examples: My boss is amenable to working from home on Fridays.
They seemed amenable to a lower price.

senses.head: Able to be treated or dealt with in a particular way
examples: The condition is amenable to surgery.
Not every problem is amenable to a quick fix.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb, with to

entries.meaning: Officially changed to correct or improve it. ---
examples: You'll need to file an amended tax return.
The committee passed an amended version of the bill.
Please sign the amended contract and send it back.
entries.position: attributive only — in legal writing also as amended after the noun

entries.meaning: Friendly and pleasant. ---
examples: Our new neighbor is an amiable guy who waves at everyone.
The meeting was surprisingly amiable.
He's much more amiable after his morning coffee.
entries.contrast: amiable describes a person or their manner; amicable describes an agreement or relationship between people (an amicable divorce).

entries.meaning: Friendly and without arguing, especially when settling a disagreement. ---
examples: The divorce was amicable, and they still co-parent well.
Both sides hope for an amicable agreement.
They parted on amicable terms.
entries.contrast: amicable describes an agreement or relationship; amiable describes a person (an amiable guy).

entries.meaning: Wrong, or not as it should be. ---
examples: I knew something was amiss when I saw the front door open.
Nothing seemed amiss at first.
Did you notice anything amiss in the report?
entries.position: predicative only — after be or seem, or right after something, nothing, anything
entries.contrast: In take something amiss (обидеться) and would not go amiss (не помешает) it works as an adverb; both are fixed phrases.

entries.meaning: Showing or feeling romantic or sexual desire. ---
examples: He wrote her amorous letters from overseas.
The couple got a little too amorous on the dance floor.
She turned down his amorous advances.

entries.meaning: Having no clear shape, structure or definition. ---
examples: An amorphous gray blob showed up on the scan.
The plan is still pretty amorphous.
Wellness has become an amorphous term.

entries.meaning: Amphibious has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Frogs are amphibious animals.
Tourists ride an amphibious bus that drives right into the river.
The Marines trained for an amphibious landing.
D-Day was the largest amphibious assault in history.

senses.head: Able to live or move both on land and in water
examples: Frogs are amphibious animals.
Tourists ride an amphibious bus that drives right into the river.

senses.head: Of a military operation: moving troops from the sea onto land
examples: The Marines trained for an amphibious landing.
D-Day was the largest amphibious assault in history.

entries.position: both — sense 2 only before a noun

entries.meaning: Ample has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There's ample parking behind the building.
You'll have ample time to finish the test.
The evidence was more than ample.
The minivan has ample room for five kids.
She had an ample figure and a big laugh.

senses.head: More than enough
examples: There's ample parking behind the building.
You'll have ample time to finish the test.
The evidence was more than ample.

senses.head: Large and roomy; of a person's body, full and rounded
examples: The minivan has ample room for five kids.
She had an ample figure and a big laugh.

entries.comparison: more/most — more ample, most ample; ampler and amplest are rare

entries.meaning: Building up muscle or other body tissue. ---
examples: He was banned for using anabolic steroids.
Protein triggers an anabolic response after exercise.
Some supplements claim anabolic effects they don't have.

entries.meaning: Belonging to a different period of time; out of date. ---
examples: A wristwatch in a movie about ancient Rome would be anachronistic.
The law is anachronistic and should be repealed.
Some find the tradition charming; others find it anachronistic.

entries.meaning: Anal has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The doctor checked for an anal fissure.
Dogs sometimes need their anal glands cleaned.
He's really anal about how the dishwasher is loaded.
Don't be so anal — nobody will notice the typo.

senses.head: Relating to the anus
examples: The doctor checked for an anal fissure.
Dogs sometimes need their anal glands cleaned.

senses.head: Informal: too worried about small details and neatness
examples: He's really anal about how the dishwasher is loaded.
Don't be so anal — nobody will notice the typo.

entries.position: both — sense 1 before a noun, sense 2 usually after a verb
entries.contrast: Sense 2 is short for anal retentive; it is informal and a little rude, so keep it out of work emails.

entries.meaning: Too concerned with order, neatness and small details. ---
examples: My roommate is so anal retentive that she labels the shelves.
He's an anal-retentive editor who checks every comma.
I'll admit I'm a little anal retentive about my calendar.
entries.position: both — hyphenated before a noun: an anal-retentive boss
entries.form: compound — anal + retentive, from Freud's psychology
entries.contrast: Informal and a bit rude. The short form is anal.

entries.meaning: Relieving pain. ---
examples: Aspirin has analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects.
The cream contains a mild analgesic ingredient.
Researchers are testing the plant's analgesic properties.
entries.contrast: Often a noun: an analgesic is a painkiller.

entries.meaning: Not digital; showing information with hands, dials or continuous signals. ---
examples: I still wear an analog watch.
The old TV only picks up an analog signal.
Vinyl fans say analog sound is warmer.
entries.contrast: American spelling; analogue is British. The noun analog means a similar thing (a meat analog); the adjective meaning 'similar' is analogous.

entries.meaning: Similar in some way, so that a comparison can be made. ---
examples: The situation is analogous to a patient refusing medicine.
The heart works in a way analogous to a pump.
Birds and bats have analogous wings.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb, with to
entries.contrast: Russian аналогичный is usually just similar in English; analogous is formal and points to a comparison of structure or function.

entries.meaning: Analytical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She has a very analytical mind.
He's the most analytical person on the team.
The lab uses analytical chemistry to test the water.
The report takes an analytical approach to the data.

senses.head: Good at thinking carefully and logically about things
examples: She has a very analytical mind.
He's the most analytical person on the team.

senses.head: Using or relating to analysis
examples: The lab uses analytical chemistry to test the water.
The report takes an analytical approach to the data.

entries.position: both — sense 2 mostly before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — in sense 1: more analytical, most analytical

entries.meaning: Relating to a sudden, severe allergic reaction. ---
examples: A bee sting sent him into anaphylactic shock.
She carries an EpiPen in case of an anaphylactic reaction.
Peanuts can cause anaphylactic symptoms within minutes.

entries.meaning: Without order or control; wild and chaotic. ---
examples: The first week of school was pretty anarchic.
The city felt anarchic after the storm knocked out power.
The show is known for its anarchic humor.
entries.contrast: anarchic means chaotic or wildly unconventional; anarchist describes the political movement (anarchist groups).

entries.meaning: Relating to the structure of the body. ---
examples: Leonardo made detailed anatomical drawings.
The model shows every anatomical detail of the heart.
There are small anatomical differences between the two species.

entries.meaning: Belonging to or inherited from your ancestors. ---
examples: They visited their ancestral village in Italy.
The family still owns its ancestral home in Virginia.
The tribe is fighting to protect its ancestral lands.

entries.meaning: Giving extra help or support; less important than the main thing. ---
examples: The hospital hired more ancillary staff.
Parking and meals are ancillary costs.
These duties are ancillary to your main job.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Andalusia, in southern Spain. ---
examples: We had Andalusian gazpacho in Seville.
The Andalusian coast is hot and dry in summer.
Flamenco is a big part of Andalusian culture.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a person from Andalusia, or a breed of horse.

entries.meaning: From or relating to the Andes mountains of South America. ---
examples: Quinoa is an ancient Andean crop.
They trekked through remote Andean villages.
Llamas are common in the Andean highlands.

entries.meaning: Not clearly male or female in appearance. ---
examples: The singer is known for an androgynous style.
Short hair made her look more androgynous.
The brand sells androgynous clothing for everyone.

entries.meaning: Based on personal stories rather than careful research. ---
examples: The evidence for the diet is mostly anecdotal.
We have anecdotal reports of the problem, but no data yet.
His claims are purely anecdotal.
entries.comparison: not gradable — usually with purely or largely
entries.contrast: Not funny: anecdotal evidence means people's stories, not scientific data. Russian анекдотичный (смешной, нелепый) is a false friend.

entries.meaning: Anemic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She was anemic during her pregnancy.
Anemic patients often look pale.
The economy showed anemic growth last quarter.
Sales were even more anemic than expected.

senses.head: Having too few red blood cells, so you feel weak and tired
examples: She was anemic during her pregnancy.
Anemic patients often look pale.

senses.head: Weak, with little energy or growth
examples: The economy showed anemic growth last quarter.
Sales were even more anemic than expected.

entries.comparison: more/most — in sense 2: more anemic, most anemic
entries.contrast: American spelling; British anaemic.

entries.meaning: Causing a loss of feeling or pain. ---
examples: The dentist rubbed an anesthetic gel on my gums.
The drug has a mild anesthetic effect.
Clove oil has natural anesthetic properties.
entries.contrast: Usually a noun: a local anesthetic. British spelling anaesthetic. Don't mix it up with aesthetic (эстетический).

entries.meaning: Very beautiful, good or innocent, like an angel. ---
examples: The baby has an angelic face.
She sang the solo in an angelic voice.
The kids looked angelic — until the adults left the room.

entries.meaning: Of the Church of England or the churches connected with it. ---
examples: He was raised in an Anglican family.
The Anglican bishops met in London.
The service followed the Anglican prayer book.
entries.contrast: In the US, the church in the Anglican family is called the Episcopal Church.

entries.meaning: Anglo-Saxon has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Anglo-Saxon kings ruled much of England.
Many short English words have Anglo-Saxon roots.
The town's founders were mostly Anglo-Saxon Protestants.
He changed his last name to something that sounded more Anglo-Saxon.

senses.head: Of the Germanic peoples who lived in England before 1066, or of their language
examples: Anglo-Saxon kings ruled much of England.
Many short English words have Anglo-Saxon roots.

senses.head: Of English or northern European descent, especially white Protestant Americans
examples: The town's founders were mostly Anglo-Saxon Protestants.
He changed his last name to something that sounded more Anglo-Saxon.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Angola, in southern Africa. ---
examples: Angolan oil exports fell last year.
She's married to an Angolan musician.
The stew is traditionally Angolan.

entries.meaning: Showing or feeling great pain or worry. ---
examples: We heard an anguished cry from the next room.
The parents looked anguished as they waited for news.
She wrote an anguished letter to her son.

entries.meaning: Angular has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The building has an angular modern design.
Her handwriting is tall and angular.
The new model is more angular than the old one.
He has an angular face with high cheekbones.
She was tall and angular, all elbows and knees.
Physics students learn about angular momentum.
The satellite's angular speed stays constant.

senses.head: Having sharp corners or angles
examples: The building has an angular modern design.
Her handwriting is tall and angular.
The new model is more angular than the old one.

senses.head: Of a person: thin, so that the bones show
examples: He has an angular face with high cheekbones.
She was tall and angular, all elbows and knees.

senses.head: Technical: measured by an angle
examples: Physics students learn about angular momentum.
The satellite's angular speed stays constant.

entries.position: both — sense 3 only before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — in senses 1 and 2: more angular, most angular

entries.meaning: Physical and instinctive, not controlled by thought. ---
examples: Fear is an animal instinct.
The actor had a kind of animal magnetism.
She felt a rush of animal panic in the dark.
entries.contrast: Usually a noun. In animal fat or animal rights it is a noun used as a modifier. The adjective means bodily and instinctive, as in Russian животный страх.

entries.meaning: Like an animal; wild, physical or uncontrolled. ---
examples: The crowd's behavior turned animalistic.
The dancers moved with an animalistic energy.
His animalistic grunts at the gym annoy everyone.

entries.meaning: Animated has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They had an animated discussion about politics.
He gets more animated when he talks about baseball.
Pixar makes animated movies.
The kids watch animated shows on Saturday mornings.

senses.head: Lively and full of energy or interest
examples: They had an animated discussion about politics.
He gets more animated when he talks about baseball.

senses.head: Made from drawings, models or computer images that seem to move
examples: Pixar makes animated movies.
The kids watch animated shows on Saturday mornings.

entries.position: both — sense 2 mostly before a noun
entries.comparison: more/most — in sense 1: more animated, most animated

entries.meaning: Deep enough to reach your ankles. ---
examples: The water in the basement was ankle-deep.
We walked through ankle-deep mud to get to the barn.
By morning the snow was ankle-deep.
entries.form: compound — noun + adjective: ankle + deep; same pattern as knee-deep, waist-deep
entries.contrast: Also works as an adverb: We waded ankle-deep into the creek.

entries.meaning: Annual has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The company holds an annual picnic in July.
Don't forget your annual checkup.
Her annual salary is $85,000.
The town gets about forty inches of annual rainfall.
Marigolds are annual flowers.
Plant annual herbs like basil after the last frost.

senses.head: Happening once every year
examples: The company holds an annual picnic in July.
Don't forget your annual checkup.

senses.head: Calculated over a period of one year
examples: Her annual salary is $85,000.
The town gets about forty inches of annual rainfall.

senses.head: Of a plant: living for only one year
examples: Marigolds are annual flowers.
Plant annual herbs like basil after the last frost.

entries.position: attributive only — after a verb say held every year
entries.contrast: Also a noun: an annual is a plant that lives one year, or a book published once a year.

entries.meaning: Carefully inoffensive, and so bland and dull. ---
examples: The press release was full of anodyne corporate language.
Her speech was polite but anodyne.
He gave the most anodyne answer he could think of.

entries.meaning: Different from what is normal or expected. ---
examples: The test gave an anomalous result, so we ran it again.
A January that warm is anomalous for Chicago.
Scientists could not explain the anomalous readings.

entries.meaning: Anonymous has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The money came from an anonymous donor.
The source asked to remain anonymous.
Police received an anonymous tip.
We stayed in an anonymous hotel near the airport.
Life in a big city can feel anonymous.

senses.head: With a name that is not known or not made public
examples: The money came from an anonymous donor.
The source asked to remain anonymous.
Police received an anonymous tip.

senses.head: Without any special features; impersonal
examples: We stayed in an anonymous hotel near the airport.
Life in a big city can feel anonymous.

entries.comparison: not gradable — except in sense 2: more anonymous

entries.meaning: Having anorexia, an eating disorder in which a person refuses to eat enough. ---
examples: She was anorexic as a teenager.
The clinic treats anorexic patients.
Her doctor was worried she had become anorexic.
entries.contrast: Also a noun (an anorexic), though many people prefer a person with anorexia. Calling a thin person anorexic as a joke is offensive.

entries.meaning: Responsible for something and required to explain it to someone. ---
examples: The police chief is answerable to the mayor.
You'll be answerable for any damage to the car.
No one at the agency seemed answerable for the mistake.

entries.meaning: Showing opposition or hostility. ---
examples: He's always antagonistic toward reporters.
Their relationship became openly antagonistic.
The two drugs have antagonistic effects.

entries.meaning: Of the region around the South Pole. ---
examples: Emperor penguins live in Antarctic waters.
Scientists spend the winter at an Antarctic research station.
Antarctic ice is melting faster than expected.
entries.contrast: Many Americans drop the first c sound: ant-AHR-tik. The Antarctic is also a noun for the region; the continent is Antarctica.

entries.meaning: From the period before the American Civil War. ---
examples: The tour includes three antebellum mansions.
Antebellum Southern society depended on slavery.
She teaches a course on antebellum literature.
entries.contrast: In American English it almost always means before the Civil War of 1861, especially in the South.

entries.meaning: Relating to the study of human societies and cultures. ---
examples: She did anthropological fieldwork in Guatemala.
The museum has a large anthropological collection.
The book takes an anthropological look at office life.

entries.meaning: Having a human form or human qualities. ---
examples: Mickey Mouse is an anthropomorphic character.
Ancient peoples worshiped anthropomorphic gods.
The robot's design is almost anthropomorphic.

entries.meaning: Opposed to the United States, its policies or its people. ---
examples: Protesters chanted anti-American slogans.
The editorial was openly anti-American.
The mood in the region grew more anti-American after the war.
entries.form: anti- + American; keep the hyphen and the capital

entries.meaning: Hostile to education, experts or serious thinking. ---
examples: He criticized the anti-intellectual tone of the campaign.
The show is proudly anti-intellectual.
Some worry that public debate has become more anti-intellectual.
entries.form: anti- + intellectual; the hyphen separates the two i's

entries.meaning: Hostile to or prejudiced against Jewish people. ---
examples: Someone painted anti-Semitic graffiti on the synagogue.
The comments were clearly anti-Semitic.
The group was condemned for its anti-Semitic views.
entries.contrast: Also spelled antisemitic, which many style guides now prefer. Either way it means hostile to Jews only, not to all Semitic peoples.

entries.meaning: Designed to shoot down enemy aircraft. ---
examples: Antiaircraft guns lined the harbor.
The plane was hit by antiaircraft fire.
The army moved antiaircraft missiles closer to the border.

entries.meaning: Killing bacteria or stopping them from growing. ---
examples: Wash your hands with antibacterial soap.
Honey has natural antibacterial properties.
Is this spray really antibacterial?

entries.meaning: Used or acting against cancer. ---
examples: The company is developing a new anticancer drug.
Broccoli may have anticancer benefits.
The trial compared three anticancer treatments.

entries.meaning: Happening or done because you expect something to happen. ---
examples: Therapists talk about anticipatory grief before a death.
The crowd let out an anticipatory cheer.
The central bank made an anticipatory rate cut.

entries.meaning: Disappointing because it is much less exciting than expected. ---
examples: After all the hype, the finale was anticlimactic.
The ending felt even more anticlimactic the second time.
It was an anticlimactic end to a great season.
entries.contrast: Spelled -climactic (from climax), not ✗ anticlimatic (from climate).

entries.meaning: Killing fungus or stopping it from growing. ---
examples: The doctor prescribed an antifungal cream.
Tea tree oil is said to be antifungal.
Runners use antifungal powder in their shoes.

entries.meaning: Killing germs such as bacteria and fungi, or stopping them from growing. ---
examples: Hospitals use antimicrobial surfaces in operating rooms.
The fabric is treated to be antimicrobial.
Overuse of antimicrobial drugs creates resistant germs.

entries.meaning: Designed to kill or injure people rather than destroy vehicles or buildings. ---
examples: Many countries have banned antipersonnel mines.
The bomb scattered antipersonnel fragments.
The treaty covers antipersonnel weapons only.

entries.meaning: Relating to collecting or selling old and rare things, especially books. ---
examples: He runs an antiquarian bookstore in Boston.
The fair attracts antiquarian dealers from all over the country.
She has an antiquarian interest in old maps.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: an antiquarian collects or sells old things.

entries.meaning: Old-fashioned and no longer suitable or useful. ---
examples: The office still runs on antiquated computers.
Some of these state laws are antiquated.
Their billing system is even more antiquated than ours.
entries.contrast: antiquated is negative (too old to be useful); antique is neutral or positive (old and valuable).

entries.meaning: Old and valuable, usually made a hundred or more years ago. ---
examples: We bought an antique dresser at an estate sale.
The antique clock still keeps perfect time.
Is that ring really antique?
entries.contrast: Russian античный (Greek or Roman) is ancient or classical in English; antique means old and valuable, usually over a hundred years old. Also a noun: She collects antiques.

entries.meaning: Hostile to or prejudiced against Jewish people. ---
examples: The university condemned the antisemitic posters.
Reports of antisemitic incidents rose last year.
His remarks were widely seen as antisemitic.
entries.form: anti- + Semitic, written as one word
entries.contrast: Also spelled anti-Semitic. Many style guides, including AP, now prefer the closed spelling, since there is no 'Semitism' that the word opposes.

entries.meaning: Antiseptic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Clean the cut with an antiseptic wipe.
The mouthwash has an antiseptic effect.
The new apartment felt antiseptic and unlived-in.
The hotel lobby was even more antiseptic than a hospital.

senses.head: Preventing infection by killing germs
examples: Clean the cut with an antiseptic wipe.
The mouthwash has an antiseptic effect.

senses.head: So clean and plain that it feels cold and has no character
examples: The new apartment felt antiseptic and unlived-in.
The hotel lobby was even more antiseptic than a hospital.

entries.comparison: more/most — in sense 2: more antiseptic, most antiseptic
entries.contrast: Also a noun: an antiseptic is a substance that kills germs.

entries.meaning: Antisocial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I'm feeling kind of antisocial tonight, so I'm staying in.
My brother gets more antisocial every year.
Vandalism is a form of antisocial behavior.
He was diagnosed with antisocial personality disorder.

senses.head: Not wanting to spend time with other people
examples: I'm feeling kind of antisocial tonight, so I'm staying in.
My brother gets more antisocial every year.

senses.head: Harmful to other people or to society
examples: Vandalism is a form of antisocial behavior.
He was diagnosed with antisocial personality disorder.

entries.contrast: In everyday American English antisocial usually just means unsociable (I'm feeling antisocial tonight). In law and psychology it means harmful to others.

entries.meaning: Designed to destroy or stop tanks. ---
examples: The soldiers carried antitank missiles.
The road was blocked with antitank barriers.
An antitank mine destroyed the truck.

entries.meaning: Directly opposed to or completely unlike something. ---
examples: Censorship is antithetical to a free press.
His views are antithetical to everything the party stands for.
They hold antithetical ideas about raising kids.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb, with to

entries.meaning: Designed to prevent monopolies and protect competition. ---
examples: The government filed an antitrust lawsuit against the company.
Antitrust regulators blocked the merger.
She's a lawyer who specializes in antitrust cases.
entries.form: anti- + trust, an old word for a monopoly
entries.contrast: An American term; British English usually says competition law.

entries.meaning: Acting against viruses. ---
examples: Doctors may prescribe an antiviral drug for the flu.
She took antiviral medication for her shingles.
The compound turned out to be strongly antiviral.

entries.meaning: Restless and impatient, unable to sit still. ---
examples: The kids get antsy on long car rides.
I start feeling antsy if I stay home all weekend.
The longer the meeting went, the antsier everyone got.
entries.form: -y from ants, as in ants in your pants
entries.contrast: Informal and American.

entries.meaning: Not interested and not caring; unwilling to make an effort. ---
examples: Young voters are often called apathetic.
He's totally apathetic about his grades.
The crowd gave an apathetic round of applause.

entries.meaning: Describing or looking like the total destruction of the world. ---
examples: The movie shows an apocalyptic future after a nuclear war.
After the wildfire, the town looked apocalyptic.
Some of the climate warnings sound almost apocalyptic.

entries.meaning: Widely told but probably not true. ---
examples: The story about George Washington and the cherry tree is apocryphal.
There's an apocryphal tale that Einstein failed math.
Most of those celebrity quotes online are apocryphal.
entries.comparison: not gradable — usually with probably or likely
entries.contrast: Russian апокрифический is mostly about religious texts; in everyday English apocryphal means a story is famous but probably not true.

entries.meaning: Not interested in politics, or not connected with it. ---
examples: My parents were totally apolitical.
The organization tries to stay apolitical.
It was supposed to be an apolitical event, but people argued anyway.

entries.meaning: Showing or saying that you are sorry. ---
examples: The manager was very apologetic about the mix-up.
She gave me an apologetic smile.
He sounded apologetic for calling so late.

entries.meaning: Extremely angry. ---
examples: My dad was apoplectic when he saw the phone bill.
Fans were apoplectic over the referee's call.
She was practically apoplectic with rage.
entries.takes: with + rage, anger; about or over + noun

entries.meaning: From or relating to the Appalachian Mountains or the region around them in the eastern US. ---
examples: They hiked part of the Appalachian Trail.
Her grandparents grew up in an Appalachian coal town.
Bluegrass has deep Appalachian roots.
entries.contrast: Many people from the region say ap-uh-LATCH-uhn and hear LAY as an outsider's pronunciation.

entries.meaning: Shocked and upset by something very bad. ---
examples: I was appalled at the condition of the kitchen.
She gave him an appalled look.
We were appalled to learn that nobody had called for help.
entries.takes: at or by + noun; to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.form: -ed — how you feel; from the verb appall
entries.contrast: appalled is how you feel; appalling is what causes the feeling. The American spelling of the verb is appall.

entries.meaning: Appalling has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The prisoners lived in appalling conditions.
It's appalling that children are going hungry.
The service at that restaurant was appalling.
His spelling is even more appalling than mine.

senses.head: Shocking and morally very bad
examples: The prisoners lived in appalling conditions.
It's appalling that children are going hungry.

senses.head: Informal: very bad in quality
examples: The service at that restaurant was appalling.
His spelling is even more appalling than mine.

entries.form: -ing — what causes the feeling; from the verb appall
entries.contrast: appalling is what causes the feeling; appalled is how you feel.

entries.meaning: Attractive or interesting. ---
examples: The job offer is very appealing.
Lower prices make the plan more appealing to families.
She has an appealing smile.
entries.contrast: Nothing to do with a court appeal: Russian апелляционный is appellate. appeal to means attract: The idea appeals to me.

entries.meaning: Relating to appeals, in which a higher court reviews a lower court's decision. ---
examples: The case went to an appellate court.
She's an appellate lawyer in Washington.
The appellate judges overturned the conviction.

entries.meaning: Looking or smelling good enough to make you want to eat. ---
examples: The dishes in the menu photos look very appetizing.
An appetizing smell came from the kitchen.
Cold, soggy fries aren't very appetizing.

entries.meaning: Relevant to or affecting a particular person or situation. ---
examples: The rules are applicable to all employees.
Fill in your middle name, if applicable.
Contractors must follow all applicable safety laws.
entries.contrast: Also stressed uh-PLIK-uh-buhl. On forms, N/A stands for not applicable.

entries.meaning: Used for practical purposes rather than studied only as theory. ---
examples: She has a degree in applied mathematics.
The lab focuses on applied research, not basic science.
Applied linguistics looks at real problems like language teaching.
entries.type: classifying — used in practice, not only in theory
entries.position: attributive only — applied math; after a verb applied is the verb: The rule was applied

entries.meaning: Appointed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The appointed judge will serve for life.
Most school board members here are elected, not appointed.
The mayor's appointed adviser resigned after a month.
We met at the appointed time.
Everyone gathered at the appointed place outside the station.

senses.head: Chosen for a job by someone in authority, not elected
examples: The appointed judge will serve for life.
Most school board members here are elected, not appointed.
The mayor's appointed adviser resigned after a month.

senses.head: Decided or agreed on in advance
examples: We met at the appointed time.
Everyone gathered at the appointed place outside the station.

entries.position: attributive only — an appointed official, at the appointed time; after a verb it is the passive: She was appointed
entries.contrast: well-appointed is a different idea: a room or hotel that is well furnished and equipped.

entries.meaning: Large or important enough to be noticed or measured. ---
examples: There was no appreciable difference between the two brands.
The new law had an appreciable effect on traffic deaths.
The change in temperature was small but appreciable.

entries.meaning: Appreciative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We're very appreciative of your help.
She wrote an appreciative note to the nurses.
The kids could be a little more appreciative of what they have.
The band played to an appreciative crowd.
He's an appreciative reader of old science fiction.

senses.head: Feeling or showing thanks
examples: We're very appreciative of your help.
She wrote an appreciative note to the nurses.
The kids could be a little more appreciative of what they have.

senses.head: Enjoying something and understanding its value
examples: The band played to an appreciative crowd.
He's an appreciative reader of old science fiction.

entries.meaning: Worried or a little afraid that something bad will happen. ---
examples: I was apprehensive about starting a new job.
She gave me an apprehensive look.
Voters grew more apprehensive as prices kept rising.
entries.takes: about or of + noun or -ing; that-clause
entries.contrast: It means worried about what may happen, not understanding: the verb apprehend means to arrest, and only rarely to grasp.

entries.meaning: Approachable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Our new manager is really approachable.
Try to seem more approachable at the front desk.
She's the most approachable professor in the department.
The book makes physics approachable for teenagers.
It's an approachable wine that goes with almost anything.

senses.head: Friendly and easy to talk to
examples: Our new manager is really approachable.
Try to seem more approachable at the front desk.
She's the most approachable professor in the department.

senses.head: Easy to understand or enjoy, even for beginners
examples: The book makes physics approachable for teenagers.
It's an approachable wine that goes with almost anything.

entries.meaning: Right or suitable for a particular situation. ---
examples: Jeans aren't appropriate for a job interview.
Please take appropriate action.
A handshake would have been more appropriate than a hug.
entries.takes: for or to + noun; to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.contrast: The verb appropriate (uh-PROH-pree-ayt) means to take something for yourself, often without permission. The adjective ends in -uht.

entries.meaning: Officially accepted as good enough or allowed. ---
examples: Use only approved chargers with this phone.
Is this car seat approved for airplanes?
Pick a book from the approved reading list.

entries.meaning: Showing that you think someone or something is good. ---
examples: Her dad gave an approving nod.
The critics were mostly approving.
My parents were never very approving of my friends.

entries.meaning: Close to the correct number or amount, but not exact. ---
examples: What's the approximate cost of the repair?
The approximate driving time is four hours.
These numbers are only approximate.
entries.contrast: The verb approximate (uh-PRAHK-suh-mayt) means to come close to. The adjective ends in -muht.

entries.meaning: Living in water or happening in water. ---
examples: Frogs and turtles are aquatic animals.
The city built a new aquatic center with three pools.
Some of these plants are fully aquatic.
entries.contrast: Also said uh-KWAH-tik. Aquatic is for living things and activities; ordinary water covers most other uses: a water bottle, not ✗ an aquatic bottle.

entries.meaning: Related to Arabia, the peninsula between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. ---
examples: The Arabian Peninsula is mostly desert.
She rides an Arabian horse.
Oman lies on the Arabian Sea.
entries.contrast: Arabian is for the Arabian Peninsula and a few fixed names (an Arabian horse, the Arabian Sea, Arabian Nights). For people use Arab; for the language use Arabic: ✗ Arabian language → Arabic.

entries.meaning: Good for growing crops. ---
examples: Only a small part of the country is arable land.
The farm has two hundred acres of arable fields.
Much of the soil there is too salty to be arable.

entries.meaning: Chosen or done by chance or personal whim, not for a reason. ---
examples: The age limit seems completely arbitrary.
Workers complained about arbitrary rules.
The new deadline is even more arbitrary than the old one.
entries.contrast: Not арбитражный. It means based on chance or someone's whim, not on a reason.

entries.meaning: Known or understood by very few people; hard to understand. ---
examples: The tax code is full of arcane rules.
He has an arcane knowledge of baseball statistics.
The debate got more arcane as the night went on.

entries.meaning: Related to archaeology, the study of the past through old objects and buildings. ---
examples: The site is an important archaeological find.
Students joined an archaeological dig in New Mexico.
The museum shows archaeological evidence of early farming.
entries.contrast: American writing also uses the spelling archeological; both are correct in the US.

entries.meaning: Very old or old-fashioned, and no longer in ordinary use. ---
examples: The state still has some archaic laws on the books.
Thou is an archaic word for you.
Their billing system is even more archaic than ours.

entries.meaning: Shaped like an arch, curving up in the middle. ---
examples: The church has tall arched windows.
She raised one arched eyebrow.
The cat's back was arched and its tail was puffed up.

entries.meaning: Being a perfect, typical example of something. ---
examples: It's the archetypal small Midwestern town.
He was the archetypal self-made businessman.
Few stories are more archetypal than the hero's journey.

entries.meaning: Related to architecture or the design of buildings. ---
examples: Chicago is famous for its architectural history.
The house has some unusual architectural details.
She works at an architectural firm downtown.

entries.meaning: Related to or kept in an archive of old records. ---
examples: The documentary uses a lot of archival footage.
Researchers spent weeks in the archival collections.
Print the photos on archival paper so they don't fade.

entries.meaning: Arctic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Polar bears live on the Arctic sea ice.
The Arctic Ocean is warming fast.
They joined an Arctic research expedition.
An arctic blast hit the Midwest this week.
The office air conditioning is arctic.

senses.head: Related to the area around the North Pole
examples: Polar bears live on the Arctic sea ice.
The Arctic Ocean is warming fast.
They joined an Arctic research expedition.

senses.head: Extremely cold
examples: An arctic blast hit the Midwest this week.
The office air conditioning is arctic.

entries.contrast: Many Americans drop the first c: AHR-tik. In the 'very cold' sense it is often written with a small letter: arctic air.

entries.meaning: Showing strong, eager feelings of support or love. ---
examples: He's an ardent supporter of gun control.
She has been an ardent Yankees fan since childhood.
Even his most ardent admirers were disappointed.

entries.meaning: Very hard and tiring, needing a lot of effort. ---
examples: It was an arduous climb to the top.
Getting a green card can be a long and arduous process.
The return trip was even more arduous.

entries.meaning: From or related to Argentina. ---
examples: We had dinner at an Argentine steakhouse.
The Argentine team won the World Cup.
Her mother is Argentine and her father is Canadian.
entries.contrast: Argentinian means the same and is common in the US. The ending is also said -tyn (AHR-juhn-tyn).

entries.meaning: Arguable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's arguable that the old system worked better.
She has an arguable claim to the land.
Whether the plan saved any money is arguable.
The referee made an arguable call in the last minute.

senses.head: Possible to support with good reasons
examples: It's arguable that the old system worked better.
She has an arguable claim to the land.

senses.head: Not certain; open to disagreement
examples: Whether the plan saved any money is arguable.
The referee made an arguable call in the last minute.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: It is arguable that…
entries.contrast: Two opposite-looking uses: it's arguable that he was right means you can make a good case that he was right; whether it worked is arguable means it is open to doubt. The adverb arguably (arguably the best) is far more common.

entries.meaning: Argumentative has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He gets argumentative when he's tired.
She's the most argumentative person in the family.
For homework, write an argumentative essay on school uniforms.
The article is more argumentative than informative.

senses.head: Often starting arguments or disagreeing with people
examples: He gets argumentative when he's tired.
She's the most argumentative person in the family.

senses.head: Presenting reasons to support an opinion
examples: For homework, write an argumentative essay on school uniforms.
The article is more argumentative than informative.

entries.meaning: Arid has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Much of Arizona has an arid climate.
Cactuses grow well in arid regions.
The land gets more arid the farther west you drive.
The report was long and arid.
He found the lectures intellectually arid.

senses.head: Having very little rain; too dry for many plants
examples: Much of Arizona has an arid climate.
Cactuses grow well in arid regions.
The land gets more arid the farther west you drive.

senses.head: Dull and without life or interest
examples: The report was long and arid.
He found the lectures intellectually arid.

entries.meaning: Aristocratic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She comes from an old aristocratic family.
The novel is set in aristocratic circles of 19th-century Russia.
He had a thin, aristocratic face.
Her manners were even more aristocratic than her mother's.

senses.head: Belonging to the highest social class
examples: She comes from an old aristocratic family.
The novel is set in aristocratic circles of 19th-century Russia.

senses.head: Looking or behaving like an aristocrat: elegant, proud, or superior
examples: He had a thin, aristocratic face.
Her manners were even more aristocratic than her mother's.

entries.comparison: more/most — more aristocratic, most aristocratic, in the 'manner' sense

entries.meaning: Related to the Greek philosopher Aristotle or his ideas. ---
examples: The course begins with Aristotelian logic.
His argument follows an Aristotelian model of ethics.
Aristotelian ideas shaped medieval science.

entries.meaning: Armed has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Two armed men robbed the store.
Police said the suspect was armed and dangerous.
Should school guards be armed?
He is serving time for armed robbery.
The armed conflict has lasted ten years.
She came to the meeting armed with facts.
We went out armed with sunscreen and bug spray.

senses.head: Carrying a weapon, especially a gun
examples: Two armed men robbed the store.
Police said the suspect was armed and dangerous.
Should school guards be armed?

senses.head: Involving the use of weapons
examples: He is serving time for armed robbery.
The armed conflict has lasted ten years.

senses.head: Having the tools or knowledge you need
examples: She came to the meeting armed with facts.
We went out armed with sunscreen and bug spray.

entries.position: both — in the 'involving weapons' sense only before a noun: armed robbery

entries.meaning: From or related to Armenia, its people or its language. ---
examples: Los Angeles has a large Armenian community.
We ordered Armenian flatbread.
Her grandparents were Armenian.

entries.meaning: Covered with armor or a hard protective layer. ---
examples: An armored truck picks up cash from the bank.
The army sent in armored vehicles.
Armadillos are armored with bony plates.
entries.contrast: American spelling; British English writes armoured.

entries.meaning: Having a strong, pleasant smell. ---
examples: The kitchen was full of aromatic spices.
Fresh basil is very aromatic.
Toasting the cumin makes it even more aromatic.

entries.meaning: Happening all day and all night without stopping. ---
examples: My grandmother needs around-the-clock care.
The hospital has around-the-clock security.
Crews did around-the-clock repairs after the storm.
entries.position: attributive only — with hyphens before a noun; after a verb it is the adverb phrase around the clock, without hyphens
entries.contrast: The store is open around the clock is an adverb phrase. Only before a noun (around-the-clock care) is it an adjective. British English prefers round-the-clock.

entries.meaning: Aroused has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The article explains what happens in the body when people feel aroused.
Some medications make it harder to become aroused.
An aroused public demanded answers.
The dog was fully aroused and barking at the door.

senses.head: Sexually excited
examples: The article explains what happens in the body when people feel aroused.
Some medications make it harder to become aroused.

senses.head: Stirred up to strong feeling or action
examples: An aroused public demanded answers.
The dog was fully aroused and barking at the door.

entries.contrast: Aroused as an adjective usually means sexually excited, so be careful with it. For interest or suspicion use the verb: The noise aroused his suspicion.

entries.meaning: Planned in advance by other people, especially a marriage chosen by the families. ---
examples: Her parents had an arranged marriage.
Arranged marriages are still common in some countries.
The two leaders met at an arranged location.
entries.position: attributive only — an arranged marriage; after a verb it is the passive: The meeting was arranged

entries.meaning: So striking that it catches your attention. ---
examples: She has arresting green eyes.
The magazine cover was bold and arresting.
It's one of the most arresting photos of the war.
entries.contrast: An arresting image has nothing to do with the police; it grabs your attention. The arresting officer is different: the officer who made the arrest, before a noun only.

entries.meaning: Acting as if you are better or more important than other people. ---
examples: He's smart but incredibly arrogant.
I didn't like her arrogant tone.
Success made him even more arrogant.

entries.meaning: Artful has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The film is an artful mix of comedy and drama.
The chef's plates were small and artful.
He gave an artful answer that avoided the question.
She was the most artful negotiator in the room.

senses.head: Done with skill and cleverness
examples: The film is an artful mix of comedy and drama.
The chef's plates were small and artful.

senses.head: Clever at getting what you want, often by tricking people
examples: He gave an artful answer that avoided the question.
She was the most artful negotiator in the room.

entries.contrast: Not the same as artistic. Artful is about skill, and sometimes about clever tricks.

entries.meaning: Having arthritis, a disease that makes joints painful and stiff. ---
examples: Our old dog has arthritic hips.
Her hands are too arthritic to open jars.
His knees got more arthritic every winter.

entries.meaning: Related to the stories of King Arthur and his knights. ---
examples: She teaches a class on Arthurian legends.
Merlin is a famous Arthurian character.
The movie is a loose retelling of an Arthurian tale.

entries.meaning: Articulate has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She's a smart, articulate speaker.
He's much more articulate in writing than in person.
The lawyer gave an articulate argument.
It was the most articulate explanation of the problem I've heard.

senses.head: Able to express ideas clearly and well
examples: She's a smart, articulate speaker.
He's much more articulate in writing than in person.

senses.head: Expressed clearly and easy to understand
examples: The lawyer gave an articulate argument.
It was the most articulate explanation of the problem I've heard.

entries.contrast: The verb articulate (ahr-TIK-yuh-layt) means to express or pronounce clearly. The adjective ends in -luht.

entries.meaning: Artificial has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The drink has no artificial colors.
We put up an artificial Christmas tree this year.
Artificial intelligence is changing a lot of jobs.
She gave me a big, artificial smile.
The conversation felt stiff and artificial, even more artificial than the last one.

senses.head: Made by people, often as a copy of something natural
examples: The drink has no artificial colors.
We put up an artificial Christmas tree this year.
Artificial intelligence is changing a lot of jobs.

senses.head: Not sincere or natural in behavior
examples: She gave me a big, artificial smile.
The conversation felt stiff and artificial, even more artificial than the last one.

entries.comparison: more/most — more artificial, most artificial, in the 'not sincere' sense; not gradable in the 'man-made' sense

entries.meaning: In Nazi and white-supremacist ideology, belonging to a supposed superior white race. ---
examples: The Nazis promoted a false myth of an Aryan master race.
The prison gang calls itself an Aryan brotherhood.
Historians explain how the idea of Aryan superiority was invented.
entries.contrast: Today the word is tied to Nazi and white-supremacist ideas about a 'pure' white race, so it appears mostly in history books and news about hate groups. Scholars now say Indo-Iranian or Indo-European for the old linguistic sense.

entries.meaning: Becoming more powerful or influential. ---
examples: The party's younger wing is now ascendant.
Streaming is the ascendant force in entertainment.
By the 1980s, the conservative movement was ascendant.
entries.contrast: In the ascendant uses the noun and means the same: Her career is in the ascendant. Sometimes spelled ascendent.

entries.meaning: Going up, or arranged from the lowest or smallest to the highest or largest. ---
examples: List the numbers in ascending order.
Sort the prices from low to high, in ascending order.
The song ends on an ascending scale.

entries.meaning: Living a very simple life without comfort or pleasure, often for religious reasons. ---
examples: The monks lead an ascetic life.
His apartment was clean and almost ascetic.
She became more ascetic as she got older.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with aesthetic (es-THET-ik), which is about beauty. An ascetic is also a noun: a person who lives this way.

entries.meaning: Asexual has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Some starfish use asexual reproduction.
Many plants can reproduce in an asexual way.
He came out as asexual in college.
The show has an asexual main character.

senses.head: In biology, happening without two parents or sex cells
examples: Some starfish use asexual reproduction.
Many plants can reproduce in an asexual way.

senses.head: Not feeling sexual attraction to other people
examples: He came out as asexual in college.
The show has an asexual main character.

entries.meaning: Very pale gray, especially of a face, from shock, fear or illness. ---
examples: His face went ashen when he heard the news.
She walked out of the doctor's office looking ashen.
The ashen sky warned of more smoke from the fires.

entries.meaning: Extremely stupid or silly. ---
examples: That's the most asinine rule I've ever heard.
He made an asinine comment about her weight.
The whole argument was asinine.
entries.contrast: From Latin asinus, 'donkey'. It is strong and insulting.

entries.meaning: Not straight or not in the right position. ---
examples: His tie was askew.
The picture on the wall hung slightly askew.
She came in with her glasses askew.
entries.position: predicative only — also after an object: The wind knocked his hat askew
entries.contrast: Russian uses an adverb (криво, набок); English uses askew after be or after an object, never before a noun: ✗ an askew picture → a crooked picture.

entries.meaning: Hoping and working to become a particular kind of person. ---
examples: She's an aspiring actress in Los Angeles.
The workshop is for aspiring writers.
Aspiring doctors have to study for years.

entries.meaning: Confident and direct in saying what you want or think. ---
examples: You need to be more assertive in meetings.
She took an assertive approach to the negotiations.
He's quiet, but he can be assertive when it matters.
entries.contrast: In American English assertive is usually a compliment: confident and clear, not rude. Aggressive is the negative word.

entries.meaning: Working very carefully and with steady effort. ---
examples: She's an assiduous student who never misses class.
Thanks to assiduous research, the reporter found the documents.
He was the most assiduous note-taker in the room.

entries.meaning: Given to a particular person as their place, share or task. ---
examples: Please go to your assigned seats.
Did you finish the assigned reading?
Parking at our office is assigned, so don't take someone else's spot.

entries.meaning: Helping and working under the person in charge. ---
examples: He works as an assistant manager at a grocery store.
The assistant coach took over after the head coach quit.
She was hired as an assistant professor of history.
entries.contrast: As a noun (my assistant) it is a person. Before a job title it means second in rank: assistant manager is заместитель управляющего. In US universities an assistant professor is a junior professor, below associate professor.

entries.meaning: Done or provided with help from another person or a machine. ---
examples: My grandfather moved into an assisted living facility.
The car has power-assisted steering.
The clinic offers assisted reproduction for couples.
entries.contrast: Assisted living is a US term for housing where older people get help with daily tasks but do not need a nursing home.

entries.meaning: Designed to help people with disabilities do things. ---
examples: Screen readers are a kind of assistive technology.
The school provides assistive devices for students who need them.
Hearing aids are the most common assistive device.

entries.meaning: Having a position just below the top rank, or less than full membership. ---
examples: She was promoted to associate professor.
He's an associate editor at the magazine.
He got an associate degree from a community college.
entries.contrast: The verb associate (uh-SOH-see-ayt) means to connect in the mind. In US universities an associate professor ranks above an assistant professor; an associate degree is a two-year college degree. Also said uh-SOH-shee-uht.

entries.meaning: Of several different kinds mixed together. ---
examples: She brought a box of assorted chocolates.
The T-shirts come in assorted colors.
The cookies in the tin are assorted.

entries.meaning: Assumed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He lived for years under an assumed name.
She checked into the hotel under an assumed identity.
The assumed cause of the fire was a faulty heater.
The plan depends on an assumed growth rate of three percent.

senses.head: False and used to hide who you are
examples: He lived for years under an assumed name.
She checked into the hotel under an assumed identity.

senses.head: Believed to be true without proof
examples: The assumed cause of the fire was a faulty heater.
The plan depends on an assumed growth rate of three percent.

entries.meaning: Assured has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She gave an assured performance in her first big role.
He seemed more assured after a few weeks on the job.
With this win, the team's place in the playoffs is assured.
Members are assured of a seat at every show.

senses.head: Confident and calm
examples: She gave an assured performance in her first big role.
He seemed more assured after a few weeks on the job.

senses.head: Certain to happen or to be received
examples: With this win, the team's place in the playoffs is assured.
Members are assured of a seat at every show.

entries.comparison: more/most — more assured, most assured, in the 'confident' sense
entries.contrast: Rest assured is a fixed phrase: Rest assured, we'll fix it means будьте уверены.

entries.meaning: Having asthma, or caused by asthma. ---
examples: Their son is asthmatic, so they can't have a cat.
Smoke is dangerous for asthmatic children.
I heard an asthmatic wheeze from the back seat.
entries.contrast: The th in asthma and asthmatic is silent.

entries.meaning: Very surprised or shocked. ---
examples: I was astounded at how much the tickets cost.
We were astounded to hear she had quit.
The astounded crowd went silent.
entries.takes: at or by + noun; to-infinitive; that-clause
entries.contrast: Astounded is how you feel; astounding is what causes the feeling.

entries.meaning: So surprising that it is hard to believe. ---
examples: The show was an astounding success.
The amount of food they wasted was astounding.
It's the most astounding comeback in the history of the sport.

entries.meaning: Related to astrology, the belief that stars and planets affect people's lives. ---
examples: What's your astrological sign?
She reads her astrological forecast every morning.
The app gives astrological advice about dating.

entries.meaning: Astronomical has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Rents in San Francisco are astronomical.
The hospital sent us an astronomical bill.
The odds of winning are astronomical.
The observatory has an astronomical telescope open to the public.
Astronomical data showed a new planet.

senses.head: Extremely large, especially of prices or amounts
examples: Rents in San Francisco are astronomical.
The hospital sent us an astronomical bill.
The odds of winning are astronomical.

senses.head: Related to astronomy, the study of stars and planets
examples: The observatory has an astronomical telescope open to the public.
Astronomical data showed a new planet.

entries.position: both — in the 'science' sense only before a noun
entries.comparison: not gradable — in the 'huge' sense it is extreme: absolutely astronomical, truly astronomical
